If none improves, investigate the policy's decisions and information rather than treating this as proof that one-frame training cannot help.

experiments.doing: Select 10 weak seeds by a recorded rule from the preceding screen and 10 randomly chosen control seeds. Run each 32 times with the frozen policy and distinct registered controller randomness: 640 complete games. These selected cases are diagnostic, not a new estimate of population performance. Record action probabilities, chosen actions, player motion, score and pickups, visible hazards, center dwell time, and first fatal contact. Measure center dwell from observed position history; any native timer used to validate telemetry stays diagnostic-only.
experiments.expected: Some seeds may produce both short failures and long successes, pointing toward action-dependent variability. Others may repeatedly produce the same failure, pointing toward a reproducible policy weakness. The sampling hypothesis predicts harmful choices where substantial probability already belongs to better actions. The risky-scoring hypothesis predicts failures clustered around particular score or pickup events. The memory hypothesis predicts outcome differences associated with recent center occupancy even in similar current observations.

If useful actions have little policy probability, learning or representation becomes a stronger lead. If every tested action fails, move the branch point earlier to investigate how the policy entered trouble. The finite set of branches does not establish an optimal action or an unavoidable death.
